claim: Music Ally computed derived population counts by multiplying Linktree's survey percentages against Linktree's separately-constructed 200 million TAM estimate, producing figures such as 68 million full-time creators and 8.2 million earning over $50,000 that neither Linktree methodology supports.
stance_target: Derived creator population counts circulated in press coverage of the Linktree report
scope_conditions: Linktree's 200 million figure comes from a top-down platform follower-bucket desk estimate while the 34%/12% percentages come from a self-selected survey of 9,576 Linktree users; the two populations are not the same, so the multiplication is invalid
quoted_support: only 34% of creators consider themselves to be working full-time on this – still around 68 million people – and of those, only 12% are making more than $50k a year from this work. That's around 8.2 million people.

claim: Spotify's platform-disclosed data provides a measured comparison to survey-based creator statistics: of roughly 2.6 million artists who uploaded at least 10 tracks, only 165,000 (6.3%) reached 10,000 or more monthly listeners, and 16,500 artists generated more than $50,000 in Spotify royalties in 2020.
stance_target: The claim that measured platform telemetry shows far lower success rates than self-selected creator surveys report
scope_conditions: Spotify only, 2020 royalty year; royalties are generated by the artists' music but paid to rightsholders, so they are not equivalent to artist take-home earnings; Spotify accounts for roughly 30% of global recorded music revenue, so total artist income is higher
quoted_support: It calculated that around 2.6 million artists had uploaded at least 10 tracks to its platform, but only 165,000 of them were reaching at least 10,000 monthly listeners – around 6.3%. ... Spotify says that in 2020, 16,500 artists generated more than $50k a year in royalties from its service
time_period: 2020 royalty year; Spotify Loud & Clear published March 2022

claim: Spotify estimated the global community of professionally aspiring music artists at roughly 200,000, three orders of magnitude below Linktree's 200 million creator estimate, illustrating how narrowly versus broadly the creator population can be defined.
stance_target: The claim that creator population estimates diverge by orders of magnitude purely because of definitional scope
scope_conditions: Spotify's March 2022 estimate based on activity on its service plus external sources such as concert listings; music artists only, not all content creators
quoted_support: Spotify suggested in March that the global community of 'professionally aspiring' music acts was around 200,000 artists, based on activity on its service as well as on external sources (like concert listings).

claim: Linktree's own follower-bucket model implies that 45 million of its 200 million creators — 22.5% — have more than 10,000 followers, a success rate roughly 3.6 times higher than Spotify's measured 6.3% of artists reaching 10,000 monthly listeners.
stance_target: The plausibility of Linktree's creator population distribution
scope_conditions: Comparison of Linktree's desk-estimated follower buckets against Spotify's measured listener telemetry; follower counts and monthly listeners are not identical metrics, so the comparison is indicative rather than exact
quoted_support: Linktree's report estimates that of the 200 million 'creators' operating on social media, 45 million have more than 10,000 followers – 22.5%.
